entries.test: Public financial and operational evidence showing whether Microsoft or OpenAI can make generative AI profitable without around-the-clock user surveillance would test the claimed necessity.
entries.note: Marcus quotes his own earlier claim approvingly. The exclusive profitability claim has a factual reading.

entries.test: An audit of Marcus's publicly recorded AI warnings over the preceding several years against subsequent events would show whether virtually all came true.
entries.note: The surrounding context supports interpreting the warnings as AI warnings. The broad quantifier does not prevent checking the record.
“Seems plausible” explicitly endorses a possibility. The extracted proposition captures that hedge rather than the separate judgment about irony.

entries.test: Public reporting and device specifications or technical documentation would establish whether OpenAI is developing continuous-monitoring devices designed to upload everything users say for cloud AI analysis.
entries.note: The main assertion concerns current device development. “No doubt” firmly endorses the upload assertion.

entries.test: OpenAI's public statements and relevant contractual language would show whether it declined to rule out surveillance of US citizens for the US government.
entries.note: The description of the language as evasive is evaluative, but the alleged refusal is a checkable factual core.
This expresses Marcus's privacy assessment without specifying a concrete data practice or privacy violation. The plugin is the immediate referent.
